reference.source: Campbell-Walsh-Wein Urology / WHO laboratory manual for semen analysis
clinicalPearls: Oligospermia denotes a sperm concentration below the lower reference limit of the WHO semen-analysis framework and is a description, not a diagnosis in itself

At least two properly collected semen samples, taken after a defined period of abstinence and analysed by WHO methods, are needed before drawing conclusions because output varies considerably over time
Causes are best organised as pre-testicular (endocrine), testicular (spermatogenic), and post-testicular (partial obstruction or ejaculatory) so that the evaluation is systematic
A hormonal profile of testosterone, luteinising hormone, follicle-stimulating hormone, and prolactin helps localise the problem; a raised follicle-stimulating hormone signals impaired spermatogenesis
Varicocele is a common and potentially correctable contributor and should be sought on scrotal examination and confirmed on ultrasound if in doubt
Modifiable factors such as heat exposure, obesity, smoking, alcohol, anabolic steroids, and certain medications should be identified and addressed
Where numbers remain too low for natural or intrauterine conception, assisted reproduction with intracytoplasmic sperm injection offers an effective route to fatherhood
Severe oligospermia warrants karyotype and Y-chromosome microdeletion testing before assisted conception because of the genetic implications for offspring
reference.pathophysiology: A reduced sperm concentration results from disturbance at one or more levels of male reproductive function. Pre-testicular causes are endocrine, with deficient gonadotropin drive (as in hypogonadotropic hypogonadism or hyperprolactinaemia) reducing the hormonal stimulation of the testis. Testicular causes involve the seminiferous epithelium itself and include varicocele, prior cryptorchidism, chromosomal or Y-microdeletion defects, gonadotoxic exposures, and idiopathic spermatogenic failure, typically accompanied by a compensatory rise in follicle-stimulating hormone. Post-testicular causes reflect partial obstruction of the excurrent ducts or ejaculatory dysfunction that reduces the number of sperm reaching the ejaculate. In many men the cause is multifactorial or remains unexplained despite full assessment.
additionalDifferentials: Gonadotoxic exposure including anabolic steroids, chemotherapy, or heat
additionalInvestigations: Repeat semen analysis by WHO methodology after a standardised abstinence interval
Endocrine profile including testosterone, luteinising hormone, follicle-stimulating hormone, and prolactin
Scrotal and, where indicated, transrectal ultrasound to detect varicocele or ductal pathology
Karyotype and Y-chromosome microdeletion analysis in severe oligospermia
Assessment of reversible lifestyle and occupational factors
Post-ejaculatory urine examination if a component of retrograde ejaculation is suspected
Cystic-fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator gene testing when ductal or seminal-vesicle abnormalities are found
redFlags: A testicular mass identified during scrotal examination or on ultrasound
Symptoms or signs of a pituitary lesion such as visual disturbance or headache
Very low sperm counts with markedly raised follicle-stimulating hormone indicating severe spermatogenic failure
Sudden deterioration in a previously normal count prompting a search for a new insult
reference.prognosis: The outlook depends on the underlying cause and severity; correctable factors such as varicocele, endocrine deficiency, or gonadotoxin exposure may improve counts, while many couples achieve pregnancy through assisted reproduction even when the concentration remains low.
pitfalls: Drawing conclusions from a single semen sample despite the wide biological variability
Neglecting a systematic pre-testicular, testicular, and post-testicular approach
Missing a correctable varicocele or endocrine cause
Proceeding to assisted conception in severe cases without genetic testing and counselling
Overlooking a partial retrograde or obstructive component reducing the count
references: WHO laboratory manual for the examination and processing of human semen
European Association of Urology guidelines on sexual and reproductive health
management: Identify and treat the underlying cause after a systematic pre-testicular, testicular and post-testicular evaluation
Correct reversible factors: weight loss, cessation of smoking, alcohol and anabolic steroids, reduction of scrotal heat exposure and withdrawal of gonadotoxic medications
Endocrine therapy where indicated, with gonadotrophin or pulsatile gonadotrophin-releasing hormone replacement for hypogonadotropic hypogonadism and a dopamine agonist for hyperprolactinaemia
Varicocele repair (varicocelectomy) in appropriately selected men with a clinical varicocele and abnormal semen parameters
Assisted reproductive techniques such as intrauterine insemination, in-vitro fertilisation or intracytoplasmic sperm injection, with surgical sperm retrieval where needed, for persistent oligospermia
Karyotype and Y-chromosome microdeletion testing in severe oligospermia, with genetic counselling before intracytoplasmic sperm injection
Avoid empirical exogenous testosterone, which suppresses spermatogenesis and worsens sperm counts
